transcript:
Header: 2025-12-02 15:10 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Carla (Redwood PM), Michael (Lumen CTO), Priya (ML Eng), Daniel (Infra), Ava (SRE)

Summary: quick deep dive into KV cache — eviction triggers, paging to host, long-context handling, prefix reuse patterns; also looked at batching/quants impacts and VPC constraints for on-prem pilot.

Topics: KV cache eviction, paging, long-token contexts, prefix reuse, batching config, quantization trade-offs, VPC/on-prem networking implications.

00:00 Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining we wanted to dig into the kv cache issues you saw in staging and try to get a repro and recommendations from Ethan. feel free to interrupt.
00:12 Michael: yep thanks samira. we've been seeing a bunch of token regen and occasional latency spikes when users hit longer sessions beyond ~16k tokens, and we suspect kv cache eviction or paging?
00:23 Priya: to add, we see sessions where prefix reuse should help a lot but the cache hit rate drops after some time and responses degrade.
00:35 Ethan: okay, can you describe the workload — are these multi-turn chat sessions with the same prompt prefixes? what's your avg seq len and the distribution?
00:48 Priya: mostly multi-turn support dialogs, initial context ~3k tokens with lots of appended user messages. avg seq is around 12k but tail goes to 40k for some cases. prefix reuse is common, we have templated instructions.
01:05 Ethan: got it — long tails. two quick calls out: first is eviction vs paging distinction, second is how batching and quantization interact with kv behavior.
01:18 Daniel: just fyi we're running on Dedicated infra (NVIDIA A100-ish) but in a VPC peered environment, and for on-prem pilot we'd be using their appliance with limited host RAM so paging to host is a real possibility.
01:33 Ethan: perfect, thanks. so eviction typically happens when the per-model per-shard kv pool reaches capacity and the runtime starts evicting LRU segments to make room — that triggers misses and you see recomputation/longer latency. paging is when we offload cold kv segments to host memory then fetch them back, which has higher but still bounded latency.
01:52 Priya: how do we tell which is happening? logs just show cache-miss spikes and increased p95 latency.
02:03 Ethan: check two things in the runtime logs — 'kv_eviction' events vs 'kv_page_to_host' markers. also look at our cache-miss histogram which correlates with token age. if evictions, you'll see items removed; if paging, you'll see page-in latencies and readback counts. we'll share exact log regexes.
02:28 Samira: note that some transcriptions of our docs call it 'kv cash' in the auto notes lol, but ignore that.
02:35 Michael: (laugh) we've seen that. okay what about prefix reuse — why would reuse not be giving sustained hits?
02:42 Ethan: a few causes — one is the shard/keying scheme: if prefixes are slightly different (timestamps, ephemeral ids) they won't match. second is cache churn from other concurrent workloads. third is when the runtime does token-level chunking for very long contexts and treats segments differently.
03:05 Priya: we do attach a session id and sometimes a last-interaction hash — could that be breaking prefix equivalence?
03:12 Ethan: yes even small differences change the hash. consider canonicalizing prompt prefixes before sending if they are templated. also we have an option to use prefix keys to force reuse — it's an API hint to the runtime. we'll send the link to docs and example code snippet.
03:32 Carla: Ethan, what about paging thresholds — can we tune those? we have limited host RAM in the on-prem config.
03:39 Ethan: yes there are tunables: max_kv_entries_per_shard, page_threshold_bytes, and eviction_policy (LRU vs LFU hybrid). for on-prem we often increase page_threshold so we page earlier rather than evict, if your host RAM allows. if host RAM is constrained you might prefer smaller active window and accept more recomputation.
03:58 Daniel: is there an automatic adaptive mode? we don't want to micromanage for every deployment.
04:05 Ethan: there's an adaptive policy in beta — it uses observed token reuse and load to adjust page vs evict thresholds. we can enable it for your pilot. but we should test it with your actual token distributions.
04:20 Michael: what about the effect of batching? our request rate is fairly bursty during peak office hours.
04:27 Ethan: batching helps throughput but increases peak memory because multiple requests' KV will be resident during batched execution. continuous batching optimization can help, but if you batch too aggressively you'll increase KV working set and risk eviction. tuning batch_window_ms and max_batch_size is key.
04:45 Priya: we use a 50ms batch window and max 8 requests; would that be too aggressive?
04:50 Ethan: 50ms with long contexts can be fine, but if each request brings a large unique context it's additive. in your case with long-tail sessions, a smaller batch size or weighted batching by seq_len might be better. we can suggest config.
05:05 Carla: quantization — does it impact kv cache size or eviction?
05:12 Ethan: quantization reduces model weights memory and runtime activations size, but kv cache is mostly activations/kv pairs; depending on implementation, quantized kernels may compress kv entries slightly but not as much as weights. however, lower-precision attention kernels can reduce per-token memory and that indirectly reduces KV working set. if you go to 4-bit quant, you may see measurable reductions in kv footprint. trade-off: some quality/regression risk.
05:40 Daniel: we plan to use int8/4-bit on Dedicated for cost. is there a recommended matrix?
05:46 Ethan: we'll share our quant recommendation table — for long-context we often keep kv in float16 but quantize weights; if you need aggressive compression you can enable kv compression (lz4) which trades CPU for smaller host pages.
06:02 Priya: can kv compression be used with paging?
06:08 Ethan: yes compressed pages reduce host transfer size and page-in latency, but adds decompression compute on page-in. if your on-prem has CPU headroom it's a net win.
06:18 Michael: ok good. let's talk reproducibility — Priya we can provide a small reproducer?
06:23 Priya: I can share two sample sessions that show the drop in hit rate, and one synthetic workload that spikes cache churn.
06:31 Ethan: perfect. please include raw token traces and request headers so we can check keying differences. also include timestamps when you saw latency spikes.
06:42 Samira: we'll also ask for logs from the runtime showing kv_eviction events and page metrics. Ethan, can you outline the exact metrics and logs we need?
06:52 Ethan: yes — kv_hit_rate (per-shard), kv_eviction_count, kv_page_in_count, avg_page_in_latency_ms, active_kv_entries, per-request memory delta, batch_size_histogram, token_age_histogram. I'll paste regex snippets and a small parsing notebook.
07:14 Priya: great, and about prefix canonicalization — should we do it client-side or can Redwood do server-side rewrite?
07:22 Ethan: we support client hints for prefix keys today; server-side canonicalization is possible but requires you to opt in since it mutates request indexing. for pilot, I'd recommend client canonicalization — it's easiest. we have examples.
07:38 Michael: VPC/on-prem networking — Daniel can you outline constraints?
07:43 Daniel: for the on-prem appliance we'll have limited egress to Redwood control plane, and peered VPC to a dedicated subnet. we need to ensure page-to-host transfers don't cross expensive links or closed subnets.
07:58 Ethan: for paging we prefer host pages to be local to the same machine or same rack. if your architecture forces page storage across peering link, page latency will be huge. for such setups we recommend either expanding local host RAM or tuning to evict more aggressively (accept recompute).
08:18 Priya: any quick wins for reducing eviction right away?
08:22 Ethan: yes — canonicalize prefixes, reduce batch max for long-context requests, enable kv compression for on-prem, and set a slightly lower max_kv_entries_per_shard to keep working set predictable. also, limit tail sequence lengths with truncation or summarize older context to reduce tokens.
08:40 Samira: we'll send a recommended config diff for your Dedicated and on-prem profiles.
08:45 Michael: what's the typical impact on latency if we page vs evict? numbers pls.
08:50 Ethan: rough order: an eviction miss costs you recomputation of keys — that can add 50–300ms depending on model and sequence segment. a page-in from local host memory typically adds 10–80ms (depending on IO and compression); remote page-in across peering could be 200–800ms, so that's the big pitfall.
09:10 Priya: okay that explains the spikes during peak when we were hitting peering.
09:14 Ethan: also watch for tiny correlated effects — big batches triggering page-in storms can spike p95.
09:22 Carla: any tools to visualize kv working set?
09:25 Ethan: yes our console has per-model kv heatmaps, per-shard active entries, and a timeline of evictions/page-ins. we'll share screenshots and a demo route for your account.
09:38 Samira: note action items again: logs/trace from Priya, infra diagram from Daniel, reproduce on staging from Ethan, Samira will send config and docs.
09:46 Michael: last Q — if we decide to go on-prem appliance, how does key management and audit look for paging and stored pages?
09:55 Ethan: pages on host are encrypted at rest with the same KMS/HSM integration; audit logs include page-in/page-out events with request ids. for air-gapped we can configure local KMS. we'll attach SOC2/ISO extracts relevant to storage and paging.
10:10 Priya: thanks. we'll prioritize the three sessions that show regressions and send them tonight.
10:16 Samira: great thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule the follow-up.

(Transcript continues with brief Q&A and some cross-talk; omitted repetitive sections)

End of call.
